To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the Ohm radius of a protostellar cloud is of the order of the size of the protostar, the magnetic field is dissipated inside this radius, the magnetic field becomes straight and uniform, and the magnetic flux dragged into the protostar is zero.

the magnetic field is dissipated inside a region of size inversely proportional to stellar mass and that the effective resistive coefficient must be higher than the microscopic resistive coefficient by at least 2 orders of magnitude.

the magnetic flux problem is avoided in our solution because the flux dragged in the central protostar is zero, and the effective resistivity in the accretion region must be higher by 1 order of magnitudes or more than the microscopic electric conductivity.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following questions: (1) What is the magnetic field structure inside an accreting protoplanetary disk? (2) What is the rate of magnetic field dissipated in the inner disk, and how does this depend on the resistivity?
the problem of the dissipation of magnetic fields in the accreton phase of low-masse star formation.
the role of magnetic fields in low-mass star-formation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the magnetic fields in star-forming regions are dissipated by the resistive effects of the gas, and the dissipation process is not a slow one.

magnetic fields are important in the early stages of low-mass protostar formation and that they may be responsible for a large part of the observed luminosity, but that their role in the formation of the final stellar mass and angular momentum is still uncertain.
the magnetic field dissipation is not a problem of star formation, but a problem of the physics of star formation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the magnetic field of the collapsing cloud is dissipated by Ohmic diffusion inside the accreting star, and the magnetic field of a T Tauri star is the same as that of the Sun, but with a polarity opposite to that of the Sun.
, in order to avoid conflict with the paleomagnetic measurements, the magnetic flux problem must be solved in a different way than by invoking magnetic field dissipation.

the magnetic field of a collapsing cloud is dissipated on the free-fall time scale, and that the dissipation occurs inside an Ohm radius that is smaller by at least an order of magnitude than that predicted by the kinematic approximation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Ohmic dissipation of the field during the accretional phase is an important process in the star formation problem.

the magnetic flux problem is not a serious obstacle to the gravitational collapse of magnetized clouds, provided that a suitable mechanism is present to dissipate the magnetic energy of the infalling material.
, if the magnetic field of molecular clouds is dissipated during the accretional phase, the magnetic flux problem is automatically solved.
